human_tolerance.notes: Large enough to raid garden fruit and to cross roads, and it basks on warm ground and low branches, so a planted plot with open soil and sunny patches suits it; it is hunted and road-killed across much of its range.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Eggs hatch at the beginning of spring; hatchlings weigh about 10 g and grow to several kilograms in four or five years, reaching reproductive maturity in their third year.

vocalizations.description: A loud, sibilant hiss with the mouth open, given as a threat display; large adults also grunt and bellow at rivals.

taxonomy.note: GBIF Backbone Taxonomy gives Squamata Teiidae and the authorship on the matched name; GBIF returns order Squamata for this species rather than a suborder.

external.note: GBIF usage key 5227370 and iNaturalist taxon id 318758, as matched by the GBIF backbone and the iNaturalist taxa API and given in issue #47.

common_names.note: English common name from Wikidata; Portuguese 'teiú-branco' from the article's interlanguage links.

range.note: Wikipedia: a large lizard of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay; formerly lumped with the Tupinambis complex as Salvator merianae / Tupinambis merianae.

traits.mass_kg.note: No trait dataset covers this species. Wikipedia gives adult females reaching 2.5-7.0 kg and a hatchling growing to 8 kg within four or five years; 4.0 kg is the midpoint of the adult female range, marked derived, and mass_range_kg carries the published span.

traits.length_m.note: Wikipedia: adult males, much larger than females, can exceed 4 ft total length including the tail at maturity.

traits.lifespan_y.note: No openly licensed source states a wild lifespan for this species; the article only notes a relatively long lifespan compared with competing species. Authored as a low-precision value for a large lizard; it is a judgement, not a measurement.

traits.diet.note: Wikipedia: the diet changes from insects in the first years to small vertebrates, eggs, carrion and fruit, and the species has one of the largest dietary ranges of any lizard. The split is authored from that sentence.

traits.social.note: No open source gives a group size; large terrestrial lizards forage alone, so Solitary [1, 1] is judgement.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Wikipedia describes daytime basking and foraging, with partial nocturnal endothermy restricted to the reproductive season.

traits.defense.note: Authored: runs off, or turns and hisses and lunges when cornered.

traits.wariness.note: Authored. Large, fast and hunted, with a high road-mortality burden, so set high.

traits.body_plan.note: Quadrupedal lizard; quadruped mesh, as for the lizard record already in this repository.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Walk and Trot chosen: a terrestrial lizard that walks when foraging and runs when threatened. It does not swim or climb, and does not fly.

traits.thermoregulation.note: Ectotherm. The article notes it is one of a few partially warm-blooded lizards, running up to 10 C above ambient at night during the reproductive season, but not a true endotherm.

traits.perching.note: Basks on low branches and fallen wood but does not perch like a bird; set to false.

traits.nest_type.note: Ground: females bury eggs in soil or use a hollow log, so Ground is the honest value.

habitat.use.note: Authored: an almost entirely terrestrial ground lizard, which the EltonTraits and PanTHERIA foraging-stratum schemes both lack a row for.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Authored: digs a burrow or uses a hollow log for shelter and overwintering, so burrow is the closest tag.

habitat.resources.note: Food weights follow traits.diet; the burrow and hollow-log shelter weight is judgement.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Authored from the species' size, its fruit diet and its basking habit, with road_mortality set High because large lizards crossing roads are a well-known hazard in Brazil.

seasonal.strategy.note: Tropical and subtropical species active year round; no true dormancy described.

seasonal.phases.note: Hatchling mass and growth to several kilograms within four or five years, and maturity in the third year, from Wikipedia; the windows are judgements.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Egg duration is judgement (a large teiid lizard's incubation is roughly two months); Juvenile duration from the four-to-five-year growth figure; scales are authored judgement.

behavior.note: Authored params for the shared ground-forager program: a long flee distance and a Trot flee gait match an animal that sprints; rest_sun_lo_deg/rest_sun_hi_deg set to -90/-6 for a diurnal basking lizard.

look.note: Colours from the species' appearance (black-and-white banded body, thick jowls, heavy tail, pale dewlap); proportions authored for a large teiid lizard with a long heavy tail, and the band, dewlap and jowl extra parts render the black-and-white banding that gives the species its common name.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: Wikipedia: adult females reach 2.5-7.0 kg and a hatchling grows to 8 kg within four or five years.

traits.shoulder_height_m.note: Authored geometry estimate for the required quadruped field: a large, heavy lizard carried low, so shoulder height is set to 0.16 m, about 13% of the 1.22 m total length. Wikipedia gives no shoulder measurement.

traits.senses.note: Authored from the species' biology: colour vision and moderate hearing and smell in a diurnal visual hunter. No open source quantifies them here.

vocalizations.hiss.note: Description from the Wikipedia behaviour section; months, time windows, cooldowns and loudness are authored judgement, as no open source quantifies them. No open source gives a frequency band, so freq_hz is omitted.
